headline: Twotree Fluke Still Producing While the Fleet Waits on the Bunker to Blow Up
subhead: Black Point sea bass are steady money right now, but every captain from Niantic to Waterford is watching the bunker schools tighten for the fall blitz.
body_markdown:
Talk at the counter this week has been less about what's biting and more about what's coming. The full moon that just crested over the weekend was the number every mate on the Niantic and Waterford boats had circled, and we flagged that back on the 4th and 5th — said the building moon toward full around September 6-7 would tighten the bunker schools and the first real blitz activity was likely within the week. That window is open now. It just hasn't cracked wide open yet.

What's actually happening: bunker are stacking thick off the mouth of the Niantic River and along the edge of Niantic Bay, and there's enough bass and blues shadowing those schools to keep rods bent, but nobody's calling it a blitz yet. It's more of a slow simmer. New London water is sitting around 69.4 degrees, which is still warm enough to keep everything comfortable and not urgent. The trigger everyone's waiting on is the new moon tide rolling in around September 10 — bigger water movement, more current push through Twotree Island Channel and Hole-in-the-Wall, and that's usually what finally forces those bunker schools to ball up tight enough for the stripers to commit instead of just picking at the edges.

For right now, fluke is still the more dependable play. Boats working Twotree Island Channel are finding keepers in 30 to 38 feet, dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with a squid strip, working the last two hours of the ebb when the current slows enough to keep bottom contact without getting swept sideways. It's not a wide-open bite — most boats are culling through a fair number of shorts to find their limit — but there are enough 3- to 5-pound fish mixed in to make the drift worth running. The morning tide has been the better window; afternoons have gotten sloppier as boat traffic picks up on the channel.

Black Point continues to be the most consistent spot on the whole beat right now. Sea bass are holding tight to the reef structure in 40 to 50 feet, and they haven't slowed down at all with the calendar turning toward fall — if anything the bite's gotten more reliable as the water's cooled a touch off the summer high. Clam and squid on a standard double-hook bottom rig, right on the structure, is still all it takes. Porgies are mixed in on the same drift, which keeps the rail busy even on days when the sea bass go quiet for a stretch.

Bluefish have been the wild card. Hole-in-the-Wall has had stretches of real chopper activity — 3- to 6-pound blues working peanut bunker pushed up against the rocks, especially on the last of an outgoing tide when the bait gets funneled through the gut. When the birds start working there, it's worth running over even if you were set up somewhere else, because that bite can shut off in twenty minutes once the blues push the bait schools out into open water. Bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig or a Hopkins jig worked through the melee both have their moments — the blues aren't picky right now, they're just aggressive.

Striped bass are the fish everybody's really asking about, and the honest answer is: they're around, they're eating, but it's not blitz behavior yet. McCook Point at last light has been giving up some slot fish to bucktails and swimming plugs worked along the drop where the bait's been holding, and there's been the occasional bigger fish mixed in chasing bunker schools off Black Point, but it's scattered — a few fish here, a missed follow there. That matches what we're hearing up and down the Sound. The bunker are there, the moon's building, the water temp is right, but the concentration that tips this into a real coastwide blitz hasn't landed yet.

Worth keeping an eye on: the albie and bonito push building through the Fishers Island Sound corridor to our east. It hasn't shown up hard inside Niantic Bay proper, but that kind of speedster activity has a habit of working west along the reef line as water temps hold in the high 60s, and this beat sits right in the path if that keeps building through the week.

Blackfish season opener is also getting closer on everyone's calendar, and a few boats have already been checking structure around Black Point and the rock piles off McCook Point in anticipation, though nothing's legal to keep yet — just scouting.

Looking ahead: if the new moon tide on the 10th does what it usually does, expect the bunker schools to tighten hard over the next several days and the bass to shift from picking to committing. That's the window worth planning around — the days bracketing the new moon, fishing the dawn and dusk push on the outgoing tide at Hole-in-the-Wall and the mouth of the Niantic River, where the current will be squeezing bait through the narrows. Fluke and sea bass should stay dependable regardless, so if the blitz doesn't materialize on schedule, Black Point and Twotree Channel are the fallback that's producing right now.
